items.title: The Arnolfini Portrait
items.creator: Jan van Eyck
facts: Hangs in the National Gallery, London, which bought it in 1842.
The Latin inscription above the mirror reads 'Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434': Jan van Eyck was here.
The convex mirror reflects two figures in the doorway, one of whom may be the painter.
items.remark: Look at the mirror: two people are standing where you are standing, and the signature above it says the painter was here. It is a witness statement as much as a portrait.
items.gaffe: Announcing that it depicts a wedding. Panofsky argued that in 1934, and art historians have been arguing about it ever since.
sources: National Gallery, London, catalogue entry NG186
Erwin Panofsky, 'Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait', Burlington Magazine (1934)

items.title: J. M. W. Turner
facts: Born in Covent Garden in 1775; entered the Royal Academy Schools at fourteen.
Rain, Steam and Speed (1844) is in the National Gallery; the bulk of the Turner Bequest is at Tate Britain.
items.remark: Turner left the nation the contents of his studio on condition it be kept together; that is why so much of him is in one building at Tate Britain.
items.gaffe: Confusing him with Constable. Constable painted Suffolk skies and hay wains; Turner painted light dissolving everything.
sources: Tate, 'Joseph Mallord William Turner 1775–1851' artist biography

items.title: The French Revolution
facts: The Bastille fell on 14 July 1789; Louis XVI was executed on 21 January 1793 and Marie Antoinette on 16 October 1793.
The Terror of 1793 to 1794 ended with Robespierre's own execution in July 1794.
Jacques-Louis David sat in the Convention, voted for the king's death, and painted the Revolution's images.
items.remark: David voted to execute the king, painted Marat dead in his bath, and then painted Napoleon's coronation; the Revolution's official artist survived every regime.
items.gaffe: Placing the storming of the Bastille in 1793. It was 1789; 1793 is the year of the guillotine.
sources: William Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution (2nd ed., 2002)

items.title: Marie Antoinette
facts: Born in Vienna on 2 November 1755, the fifteenth child of the Empress Maria Theresa.
Married the future Louis XVI in 1770, aged fourteen; guillotined on 16 October 1793.
Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun painted her some thirty times.
items.remark: She was a Habsburg first: an Austrian archduchess sent to France at fourteen, and 'l'Autrichienne' was the insult that followed her to the scaffold.
items.gaffe: Attributing 'let them eat cake' to her as fact.
sources: Antonia Fraser, Marie Antoinette: The Journey (2001)

image.source: Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, Marie Antoinette with a Rose (1783), via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (artist died 1842); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: "Let them eat cake"
facts: Rousseau's Confessions, Book VI, has the anecdote; the passage was written around 1765, when Marie Antoinette was about ten.
The French is 'qu'ils mangent de la brioche', and brioche is not cake.
items.remark: Rousseau wrote that line down when she was about ten and living in Vienna; nobody pinned it on her until well after her death.
items.gaffe: Quoting it as fact at a table where anyone has read a biography.
sources: Antonia Fraser, Marie Antoinette: The Journey (2001)
items.claim: Told that the poor had no bread, Marie Antoinette said: let them eat cake.
items.truth: The line appears in Rousseau's Confessions, attributed to 'a great princess', and was written when Marie Antoinette was a child in Vienna. No contemporary source connects it to her.

items.title: Symphony No. 5 in C minor, Op. 67, first movement
items.creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
facts: Premiered on 22 December 1808 at the Theater an der Wien, on the same marathon programme as the Sixth Symphony and the Fourth Piano Concerto.
Composed between 1804 and 1808, alongside the Fourth Symphony and the Violin Concerto.
items.remark: The 'fate knocking at the door' line comes from Beethoven's secretary Schindler, whose reliability scholars doubt; say that, and you sound like you have read something.
items.gaffe: Calling it the Fifth Piano Concerto. That is the Emperor, and it is a different piece.
sources: Lewis Lockwood, Beethoven: The Music and the Life (2003)

theme.note: Opening motif, strings and clarinets in unison. Fermatas approximated as long notes.

items.title: Lied
facts: Schubert wrote more than six hundred Lieder, including the cycles Die schöne Müllerin and Winterreise.
Schumann, Brahms, Wolf, Mahler and Strauss carried the form to the end of the nineteenth century.
items.remark: The point of a Lied is that the piano is telling the story too; listen to what it does under the voice, not just to the tune.
items.gaffe: Saying 'a Lieder'. Lied is the singular; Lieder is the plural.

term: A short instrumental piece for solo piano in a single mood, often published in sets.
A German dance in triple time that preceded the waltz.
The German term for a choral movement in an oratorio.

items.definition: A German art song for solo voice and piano, in which the piano is a partner rather than an accompaniment; the plural is Lieder.

items.title: Ombra mai fu
items.creator: George Frideric Handel
facts: Opens Serse, which premiered at the King's Theatre in the Haymarket, London, on 15 April 1738.
Known as 'Handel's Largo', though Handel marked it larghetto.
Sung by Xerxes, king of Persia, in praise of the shade of a plane tree.
items.remark: It is a love song to a tree; Xerxes is serenading a plane tree, which is why the opera was laughed at in 1738 and adored two centuries later.
items.gaffe: Calling it 'Handel's Largo' as if that were its name, or assuming it is addressed to a woman.

items.title: Royal Opera House, Covent Garden
facts: The first theatre on the site opened in 1732 under John Rich; the present building, by E. M. Barry, opened in 1858 after fires in 1808 and 1856.
Handel wrote many of his operas and oratorios for the first Covent Garden theatre.
It has been called the Royal Opera House since 1892.
items.remark: Everyone calls it Covent Garden; the current house is the third on the site, the first two having burned down.
items.gaffe: Calling it 'the Royal Albert Hall' or 'the Coliseum', which is the other opera house across the road, home of English National Opera.
sources: Royal Opera House, 'History of the Royal Opera House'

scenarios.setting: Dinner in the seventh arrondissement. The conversation has reached Versailles.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "Of course, Versailles was Louis XIV's way of keeping the nobles busy, wasn't it?"

options.text: Busy and broke. Making them live at court on his timetable was the point; the etiquette was the leash, and Saint-Simon spent forty years resenting it in his memoirs.
options.explanation: Specific, agrees where the host is right, and adds one thing they did not know (Saint-Simon's memoirs). This is the register to aim for.

options.text: It was Louis XV who built it, actually; Louis XIV preferred the Louvre.
options.explanation: Wrong. Louis XIII built the hunting lodge; Louis XIV turned it into the palace and moved the court there in 1682. Louis XV inherited it.

options.text: I have never understood why anyone bothers with Versailles. It is just a very big house.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it dismisses your host's subject and announces you have nothing to add. Philistinism is not the same as wit.
